text: Single-task results. We fine-tune one policy per task with RTC disabled to match baselines.
Kimodo-Policy uses direct task fine-tuning; Kimodo-Policy ∗ initializes ControlNet and the hand
head from our 419-hour VLA pretraining. Kimodo-Policy achieves the highest overall success rate
(SR; 69.51%), exceeding the strongest baseline, DP (Chi et al., 2023) (60.0%), by 9.51 percentage
points. It also leads in average HSI SR (84.58%) and ties Kimodo-Policy ∗ for lowest average fall
rate (AFR; 4.29%). Kimodo-Policy ∗ achieves 67.14% overall and 84.17% average HSI SR, leading
OpenDoor (93.3%) and VisNavi (76.7%). VLA pretraining improves selected tasks, while direct
fine-tuning yields higher overall SR.
Multi-task results. We jointly train one policy on all seven HumanoidArena tasks and evaluate
under SONIC (Wang et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026), with RTC disabled to match baselines. Table 2
shows Kimodo-Policy ∗ reaching 72.14% overall SR, exceeding the strongest baseline, π 0.5 (Black
et al., 2025a) (53.8%), by 18.33 percentage points, with lowest AFR (4.29%). It leads HOI (56.11%)
and HSI (84.17%) averages, P&Pbox (90.0%), OpenDoor (95.0%), SitSofa (96.7%, tied), and Vis-
Navi (76.7%). Without VLA pretraining, Kimodo-Policy reaches 67.63% overall and 51.67% HOI
SR; overall SR falls only 1.88 percentage points from single-task training. Thus, a shared policy can
retain much of its single-task performance with high success and low fall rates.
Single-task results. Table 3 evaluates VLA-pretrained Kimodo-Policy (Ours ∗ ) on eight SIMPLE
tasks, aggregating L0–L2 success rates with RTC disabled to match the baselines. It achieves best
or joint-best results on six tasks: Handover (83% vs. 80% for the strongest baseline), Mobile P&P
(70% vs. 60%), OpenOven (57% vs. 53%), OpenFaucet (53% vs. 33%), CloseDoor and Push Office
Chair (both 100%, tied with Ψ 0 ). It ranks second on XMoveBendPick (80% vs. 93% for Ψ 0 ) and
OpenTrashCan (63% vs. 83%). These results show that the motion-prior-based, visually grounded
root–body–hand policy supports handover, mobile manipulation, articulated-object interaction, and
pushing under visual, lighting, and target-pose variation.

Kimodo-Policy uses the pretrained Kimodo T2M model (Rempe et al., 2026) as its motion backbone.
To assess how prior quality affects VLA control, we compare Kimodo-G1-SEED-v1 and RP-v1
under the same policy architecture, adaptation procedure, and HumanoidArena protocol. Both have
282M parameters and 90%/10% train/test splits; SEED-v1 uses 288 h of BONES-SEED motion
data, whereas RP-v1 uses 700 h of Rigplay (Rempe et al., 2026).
T2M transfer results. Table 4 shows task-dependent gains from the stronger backbone. Overall
success rate (SR) rises from 64.29% with Kimodo-G1-SEED-v1 to 67.63% with RP-v1, a 3.34-point
improvement. RP-v1 improves DoubleDesk from 33.33% to 40.0%, P&Pbox from 75.0% to 80.0%,
OpenDoor from 60.0% to 93.3%, and SitSofa from 90.0% to 96.7%. However, Football declines
from 50.0% to 35.0%, Boxing from 71.67% to 66.7%, and VisNavi from 70.0% to 61.7%. The
aggregate gain is concentrated in human–scene interaction tasks, while individual outcomes remain
sensitive to the motion prior. With architecture and training protocol fixed, these results indicate that
stronger T2M priors can improve downstream VLA control despite task-dependent trade-offs.
We isolate data and capacity effects through two controlled sweeps, with RTC disabled to match
the benchmark protocol. The data sweep varies the duration of VLA policy-pretraining data while
fixing the architecture, SonicX7 adaptation protocol, and evaluation setting. The model sweep varies
the active policy parameter count while fixing the pretrained T2M backbone, downstream data,
optimization protocol, and evaluation suite.

Attention map analysis. Figure 5 shows Kimodo-Policy focusing on the ball in Football, box in
P&P Box, and punching bag in Boxing, alongside relevant scene elements for door opening, sitting,
and navigation. π 0.5 responds less locally, while Diffusion Policy activates broader scene regions.
This task-dependent focus suggests alignment with instruction semantics and use of task-relevant
cues for shared multi-task action selection.
Dual-Path Fusion. DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) encodes the current egocentric image into spa-
tial tokens for trainable root and body ControlNet branches. At selected layers of each Kimodo
denoiser, future-motion hidden states query these tokens through cross-attention, while a token-
axis MLP maps the image-token sequence to the future temporal horizon. Summed outputs pass
through a layer-specific zero-initialized projection, producing a residual hint for the corresponding
Kimodo layer. Hints are added only to future-motion tokens, leaving the constrained history prefix
unchanged. Zero initialization preserves pretrained behavior at adaptation onset; both paths ground
the frozen prior through content-selective visual retrieval and temporally aligned conditioning.
HandNet. Hand control specifies opening or closing rather than kinematic pose trajectories, moti-
vating a dedicated bilateral diffusion head. At each denoising step, HandNet jointly processes the
current hand state, noisy future hand controls, future body hidden states, and visual tokens to predict
two hand-control values per future frame. Conditioning on predicted body features and the current
scene aligns hand commands with whole-body action, while the separate head keeps hand labels
outside the root–body motion space. It supports binary open/close states and continuous closure
changes. During training, body and visual features are detached: hand supervision updates HandNet
without gradients to the motion denoiser or ControlNet.
The masked MSE terms L r , L b , and L h reconstruct clean normalized root–body features and hand
targets. Binary hand targets use [−1, 1]; continuous targets encode closure residuals from the latest
valid observed hand state. L ∆ computes ℓ 1 error in predicted versus demonstrated consecutive
hand-control changes, including the observed-to-first-future transition; continuous residuals are first
converted to closure values. All losses mask padding; hand losses also mask unavailable labels,
and transitions require two valid adjacent labels. The main MSE weights are (λ r , λ b , λ h , λ ∆ ) =
(4, 1, 1, 0.2). Predicted root motion and, in the main configuration, root ControlNet features are
detached before body generation; HandNet receives detached body and visual features. Kimodo
denoisers and the DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) encoder remain frozen.
Inference. Each policy query encodes the language instruction and current egocentric image, and
represents available proprioceptive history in Kimodo’s motion space with frame- and feature-wise
observation masks. DDIM (Song et al., 2022) iteratively denoises future motion and hand sequences
initialized from Gaussian noise. Each step restores observed history, injects visual features into
frozen root and body denoisers via ControlNet, conditions body generation on predicted root mo-
tion, and predicts hand controls with HandNet using the current hand state, visual features, and
future body features. After denoising, we invert the motion representation and map root and joint
trajectories, together with bilateral hand commands, to tracker-compatible references. The low-level
whole-body tracker executes a chunk prefix; the policy replans from updated images and proprio-
ceptive states, combining structured motion generation with continual closed-loop correction.
Figure 4: Motion-Prior Transfer. Top: frozen Kimodo generates a complete “Sit on the sofa”
sequence from text. Bottom: Kimodo-Policy predicts short chunks from vision and motion history
for closed-loop control. Light brown: observed history; blue: predicted and executed motion.
Motion Prior Transfer. Figure 4 illustrates how a pretrained motion prior supplies temporal struc-
ture and whole-body coordination for visually grounded control. Given only “Sit on the sofa,” Ki-
modo (Rempe et al., 2026) generates a coherent sequence ending in a seated posture (top), but lacks
grounding in the current scene and robot state. Kimodo-Policy freezes this backbone and injects
egocentric visual features through trainable ControlNet branches; motion-history constraints anchor
predictions to the ongoing trajectory, enabling the same task from visual observations and state his-
tory (bottom). Task-specific learning thus adapts reusable behavior-level structure to the instruction,
scene, and state, reducing the need to relearn basic motion patterns from robot demonstrations while
preserving coherent closed-loop execution.
Motion-History Conditioning. Fixed T2M sequences cannot respond to deviations between pre-
dicted and measured motion or scene changes. We therefore formulate each closed-loop query as
constrained motion completion in Kimodo’s kinematic representation. Observed history forms the
prefix of a history–future window, with feature-wise masks identifying available kinematic values.
The prefix is restored before each denoising step; the unconstrained future becomes the next ac-
tion chunk. Trainable ControlNet branches inject current egocentric image features into Kimodo’s
root and body denoisers, grounding predictions while retaining the pretrained root–body structure.
The tracker executes a chunk prefix; updated history and images condition the next query. This
receding-horizon loop preserves the motion prior with continual visual and state-based correction.
We evaluate Kimodo-Policy through single- and multi-task HumanoidArena control (Sec. 4.1), SIM-
PLE manipulation (Sec. 4.2), and real-world deployment (Sec. 4.3). Analyses cover T2M backbone
quality (Sec. 4.4), data and model scaling (Sec. 4.5), and design ablations (Sec. 4.6). Appendix B
details the datasets, training protocols, and evaluation environments.
HumanoidArena (Wang et al., 2026a) covers seven language-conditioned tasks spanning human–
object interaction (HOI) and human–scene interaction (HSI). We evaluate independent per-task fine-
tuning and joint training across SONIC tasks. Appendix C.1 (Fig. 11) visualizes the tasks.
